rv.q: If you can overlook the absurdity of casting the ravishing Jessica Chastain as the plain and clumsy heroine of " The Heiress ," Ruth and Augustus Goetz's 1947 stage adaptation of "Washington Square," then Moises Kaufman 's masterfully helmed production is everything you want from a Class A revival.
Ms. Ivey is a knockout, and Mr. Strathairn is always worth seeing, even when, as is the case this time around, he fumbles the interpretive ball.

Unfortunately, Chastain isn't authoritative enough. When she utters the play's most famous line — 'Yes, I can be cruel. I have been taught by masters!' — the words should hit us like a hammer. Here, they barely graze.
An underpowered Jessica Chastain, hampered by questionable directorial choices, dilutes the emotional impact of this nonetheless compelling melodrama.
Like many a Broadway chestnut roast, The Heiress is handsomely done, more than competent, and not unaffecting.

Maybe, if someone never saw the revelatory Cherry Jones in the 1995 revival of "The Heiress," well, maybe the one now starring Jessica Chastain would make the 1947 drama feel like a genuine demi-classic discovery.
Otherwise I had been reasonably content, if unstirred, listening to the plot’s oiled cylinders click into place and admiring the view.
Chastain makes for a wholly plausible and fascinating Catherine.
In her Broadway debut, Chastain conveys social discomfort and awkwardness without veering into caricature.
It’s an excruciatingly effective performance.

A strong cast under Moises Kaufman's studied and well-paced direction brings a fresh vision and new life to Ruth and Augustus Goetz's 65-year-old stage dramatization of Henry James's novel Washington Square.
Both are characters far more complex and more rewarding than mere pencil sketches; they’re oil paintings, lustrous and shaded by loneliness and self-deception.
Watching Catherine grow in resolve and self-esteem — and seeing Chastain magnificently command the stage while doing so — is perhaps the greatest pleasure of this production.
And Chastain gives her a forbearance and dignity that blossoms even after her frail glow seems in danger of being extinguished .
Fortunately, Chastain drives the forbidden love affair to a far more modern conclusion.

"The Heiress," a 1947 costume drama by Ruth and August Goetz based on the 1880. Henry James novel "Washington Square," has been revived on Broadway with the same regularity as other far more important classics of American drama.
Oscar nominee Jessica Chastain is a fine actress who seems incapable of a false move, giving a naturalistic performance, though I found some of her moments flat, needing a bit more awakened fire.

If you can set aside both of those potent forces, you’ll find "The Heiress" an appealing journey through love’s promises and regrets, though ultimately the affair between Catherine and Morris only achieves about the gravitas of a college fling—heady, for sure, but not ultimately compelling.
Catherine’s transformation from prey to predator (“I have been taught by masters,” she famously spits near the play’s end) shocks and satisfies, which is all you can ask of a matinee play.
Both give committed and persuasive, if not transcendent, performances.
In early scenes, she overplays Catherine's lack of social know-how.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this revival: Chastain's casting as the "plain" Catherine strains credibility, though many praise her subtle performance.

vs.sum: The Walter Kerr Theatre offers excellent sightlines and sound quality, making it a great venue for intimate productions. However, the comfort level is below average due to limited legroom and seat width, though the theater's Italian Renaissance-inspired decor adds to its charm.

acc.note: No elevators. All accessible seating on Orchestra level. Infrared headsets and audio induction neck loops.
